item.title: 🎨 Google Ships Generative UI in Gemini and Search — What It Means for Product Design
item.description:
Google Ships Generative UI in Gemini and Search — What It Means for Product Design

Google just made one of the boldest bets in interface design: letting an AI model generate entire interactive UIs on the fly. With Gemini 3 Pro now powering "dynamic views" inside the Gemini app and rolling out in Google Search AI Mode for US Pro/Ultra subscribers, we are watching the first major production deployment of what the industry calls Generative UI (GenUI) — interfaces that do not exist until the moment a user needs them.

What Google actually shipped

Gemini 3 Pro can now produce complete HTML/CSS/JavaScript interfaces — not canned widget templates, but novel layouts assembled from scratch. Two experiments are live in the Gemini app: one renders rich "dynamic views" (interactive charts, comparison tables, mini-apps) inline with chat responses; the other applies "visual layouts" that style text-heavy answers into scannable cards and sections. In Search AI Mode, the same capability generates bespoke result pages that adapt to query intent.

Google Research published an evaluation framework alongside the launch. Their finding: GenUI outputs were ranked just below human expert-designed websites on usefulness and visual quality, and significantly above standard text or markdown responses. The gap to human-expert parity is narrow — but it exists, and it matters.

The catches are real

Generation takes "a minute or more" for complex layouts, making it impractical for time-sensitive interactions. More critically, the same hallucination risks that plague text generation now extend to UI: a confidently rendered but factually wrong chart is arguably worse than a wrong sentence, because visual framing increases perceived credibility. Google acknowledges occasional inaccuracies and is gating the rollout accordingly.

What this means for product designers

Nielsen Norman Group published a timely framework for thinking about GenUI that cuts through the hype. Their core argument: the designer's job shifts from interface design to outcome design. Instead of specifying layouts, you specify intent — what the user should accomplish — and constraints — what must, should, or must never appear.

Three practical implications emerge:

  1. Guardrail design becomes a first-class discipline. NN/g proposes a "must show / should show / never show" framework. If your checkout flow must always display the total price and must never auto-submit, those constraints need to be formally specified — not embedded in a Figma file that an AI will never read. This is closer to writing acceptance criteria than drawing screens.
  2. Design systems gain a new consumer. Today your design system serves human developers. Tomorrow it also serves AI models assembling interfaces. That means your component documentation needs to be machine-parseable — structured metadata, clear usage constraints, explicit do/don't rules. (This dovetails with the broader "machine-readable design specs" movement we cover in a companion entry.)
  3. User research becomes more important, not less. When the interface is no longer fixed, you cannot test a single mockup. You need to understand user intent deeply enough to write outcome specifications that hold across thousands of possible generated layouts. Shallow persona work will not cut it.

The consistency problem

Every design system exists to enforce consistency. GenUI, by definition, produces variation. Google is navigating this tension by constraining generation within Material Design parameters, but the fundamental friction remains: if every query produces a unique interface, how do users build spatial memory? How do they know where to look? This is an open research question, and it is the strongest argument against shipping GenUI for high-frequency, habitual-use surfaces.

What to do now

You do not need to redesign your product around GenUI today. But you should:

  • Audit your design system documentation for machine-readability. Can a model understand your component constraints without a human interpreting them?
  • Start writing outcome specs for your most important flows — what must happen, what must appear, what must never happen — independent of any specific layout.
  • Watch Google's evaluation methodology. Their research paper introduces metrics for rating generated UIs that will likely become industry benchmarks.

GenUI is not replacing product designers. It is replacing the part of the job that was already becoming commoditized — layout assembly — and elevating the parts that were always the hard work: understanding users, defining outcomes, and setting constraints that hold under uncertainty.

Google 在 Gemini 和搜索中上线生成式 UI —— 这对产品设计意味着什么

Google 刚刚在界面设计领域下了一个大胆的赌注：让 AI 模型实时生成完整的交互界面。随着 Gemini 3 Pro 在 Gemini 应用中驱动「动态视图」，并在美国 Pro/Ultra 订阅用户的 Google 搜索 AI 模式中逐步上线，我们正在见证业界所称的生成式 UI（GenUI）的首次大规模生产部署——界面在用户需要的那一刻才被创造出来。

Google 实际发布了什么

Gemini 3 Pro 现在可以生成完整的 HTML/CSS/JavaScript 界面——不是预制的组件模板，而是从零组装的全新布局。Gemini 应用中有两个实验功能：一个在聊天回复中渲染丰富的「动态视图」（交互图表、对比表格、迷你应用）；另一个则将大段文字答案排版成易于扫读的卡片和分区。在搜索 AI 模式中，同样的能力会根据查询意图生成定制化的结果页面。

Google Research 同步发布了评估框架。结论是：GenUI 输出在实用性和视觉质量上仅略低于人类专家设计的网站，并显著优于标准文本或 Markdown 输出。与人类专家的差距很小——但确实存在，并且值得关注。

现实中的问题

复杂布局的生成需要一分钟甚至更长，这对时间敏感的交互场景不太实际。更关键的是，文本生成中的幻觉风险现在延伸到了 UI：一个看起来自信满满但实际错误的图表，可能比一句错误的文字更具误导性，因为视觉呈现会增强可信度。Google 承认存在偶发的不准确情况，并因此控制着上线节奏。

对产品设计师意味着什么

Nielsen Norman Group 发布了一个关于 GenUI 的及时框架。核心观点是：设计师的工作从界面设计转向结果设计（outcome design）。你不再指定布局，而是指定意图——用户应该完成什么——以及约束——什么必须出现、什么不能出现。

三个实际影响：

  1. 护栏设计成为一级学科。 NN/g 提出了「必须展示 / 应该展示 / 绝不展示」框架。如果结账流程必须始终显示总价且绝不能自动提交，这些约束需要被正式规范化——而不是嵌入在 AI 永远不会阅读的 Figma 文件中。
  2. 设计系统多了一个新消费者。 今天你的设计系统服务于人类开发者，明天它还要服务于组装界面的 AI 模型。这意味着你的组件文档需要机器可解析——结构化元数据、清晰的使用约束、明确的规则。
  3. 用户研究变得更重要，而非更不重要。 当界面不再固定时，你无法只测试一个原型。你需要深入理解用户意图，才能编写出在成千上万种生成布局中都成立的结果规范。

现在该怎么做

你不需要今天就围绕 GenUI 重新设计产品。但你应该：审查设计系统文档的机器可读性；开始为最重要的流程编写结果规范；关注 Google 的评估方法论——他们的研究论文引入了评价生成式 UI 的指标，很可能成为行业基准。

GenUI 不是在取代产品设计师。它取代的是工作中已经逐渐商品化的部分——布局组装——并提升了一直以来真正困难的部分：理解用户、定义结果、以及在不确定性中设定有效约束。

  • https://blog.google/products/gemini/gemini-3/
  • https://www.nngroup.com/articles/generative-ui/
  • https://x.com/Google

item.title: 🎨 From Design Systems to Product Generation Systems: ANOVA and the Machine-Readable Spec Movement
item.description:
From Design Systems to Product Generation Systems: ANOVA and the Machine-Readable Spec Movement

Design systems solved consistency at scale. The next challenge is creation at scale — and a growing community of practitioners argues that requires a fundamental shift in how we document components. The thesis: if AI models are going to assemble interfaces (as Google's GenUI work demonstrates), the specs those models consume need to be deterministic, complete, and machine-readable. Human-friendly Figma annotations are not enough.

Two recent pieces crystallize this movement: Gerard Pàmies's essay on "Product System Design" and Nathan Curtis's ANOVA plugin for Figma — a tool that quietly solves one of the hardest problems in the AI-assisted design pipeline.

The argument for Product Generation Systems

Pàmies, writing in Design Bootcamp this month, draws a clear evolutionary line. Design systems gave teams shared components, tokens, and patterns. They solved the problem of "everyone building the same button differently." But they still require a human to assemble those components into screens, flows, and products.

Product generation systems go further: they provide enough structured information that an AI agent can assemble components into coherent interfaces autonomously. The difference is not in the components themselves but in how they are documented. A design system says "here is a card component with these variants." A product generation system says "here is a card component; it must be used in these contexts, never in those; its content hierarchy is title → subtitle → body → action; spacing follows this token; it pairs with these siblings."

The key insight: documentation must shift from human-readable guidelines to machine-readable constraints. An AI model cannot interpret a Notion page that says "use generous whitespace." It needs a structured rule: min-spacing: var(--space-4); context: card-grid; exception: compact-mode.

ANOVA: deterministic specs from Figma

This is exactly the gap Nathan Curtis's ANOVA plugin fills. ANOVA extracts component specifications from Figma as structured JSON or YAML — not by asking an LLM to interpret a design, but by deterministically reading Figma's component data and producing a clean, complete specification.

Why does determinism matter? Because LLMs are inconsistent. Ask GPT or Claude to describe the same Figma component twice, and you will get different property names, different hierarchies, different levels of detail. Curtis calls this the "rename problem" — models rename properties across runs, making automated pipelines unreliable. ANOVA eliminates this by never involving an LLM in the extraction step.

The numbers are striking. Figma's REST API exposes 14,400+ properties for a typical component — most redundant or inherited. ANOVA strips this down to only the meaningful, changed properties, following four principles:

  • Deterministic — same input always produces the same output
  • Complete — captures all semantically relevant properties
  • Succinct — omits noise (inherited defaults, redundant nesting)
  • Human-readable — the output is still useful to a person, not just a machine

Seven use cases, one underlying pattern

Curtis outlines seven applications for ANOVA specs: feeding LLM prompts with accurate component data, tracking version-over-version changes, analyzing component catalog coverage, inspecting quality and consistency, powering developer handoff, auto-generating documentation, and enabling round-trip generation (design → code → design). The underlying pattern is the same in every case: a single source of structured truth about what a component is and how it behaves.

This converges with the GenUI trajectory. Google needs machine-readable component specs to constrain generated interfaces within Material Design. Any team adopting generative UI tooling will face the same requirement. The question is whether you build that structured layer proactively or scramble to retrofit it when an AI tool demands it.

What's coming next

Curtis has announced plans for an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and a CLI tool, which would let AI coding agents query component specs directly during code generation. He is also speaking at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026, which will likely push these ideas further into the mainstream design-engineering conversation.

The broader signal: the design-to-code pipeline is being rebuilt around structured, deterministic specs rather than visual interpretation. Tools like ANOVA, combined with MCP integration, create a path where AI agents can assemble interfaces with the same component fidelity a senior engineer would achieve — because they are reading the same spec, not guessing from a screenshot.

What to do now

  • Evaluate your component documentation through a machine-readability lens. Could an AI model correctly use your components based solely on your current docs?
  • Try ANOVA on a few core components and compare its output to your existing handoff specs. The delta reveals what structured information you have been leaving implicit.
  • Start thinking in constraints, not guidelines. "Use generous whitespace" is a guideline. min-gap: 16px; context: content-card is a constraint. AI agents need the latter.

Design systems were the answer to "how do we stay consistent?" Product generation systems are the answer to "how do we let AI create with our components?" The transition is already underway — the teams that structure their specs now will have a significant head start.

从设计系统到产品生成系统：ANOVA 与机器可读规范运动

设计系统解决了规模化一致性的问题。下一个挑战是规模化创造——越来越多的从业者认为，这需要从根本上改变我们记录组件的方式。核心论点：如果 AI 模型将要组装界面（如 Google 的 GenUI 所展示的），那么这些模型消费的规范必须是确定性的、完整的、机器可读的。仅靠对人类友好的 Figma 标注远远不够。

两篇近期文章集中体现了这一运动：Gerard Pàmies 关于「产品系统设计」的文章，以及 Nathan Curtis 的 ANOVA Figma 插件——一个悄然解决了 AI 辅助设计流程中最棘手问题的工具。

产品生成系统的论证

Pàmies 在本月发表于 Design Bootcamp 的文章中画出了清晰的演进路线。设计系统为团队提供了共享的组件、令牌和模式，解决了「每个人用不同方式构建同一个按钮」的问题。但组装这些组件仍然需要人类。

产品生成系统更进一步：它提供足够的结构化信息，使 AI 智能体能够自主将组件组装成连贯的界面。区别不在于组件本身，而在于如何记录它们。设计系统说「这是一个卡片组件，有这些变体」；产品生成系统说「这是一个卡片组件；它必须在这些上下文中使用，绝不能在那些场景中使用；内容层级为标题→副标题→正文→操作；间距遵循此令牌；它与这些兄弟组件配对。」

关键洞察：文档必须从人类可读的指南转向机器可读的约束。AI 模型无法解读 Notion 页面上「使用充裕的留白」这样的描述。它需要结构化规则：min-spacing: var(--space-4); context: card-grid; exception: compact-mode。

ANOVA：从 Figma 中提取确定性规范

Nathan Curtis 的 ANOVA 插件正好填补了这个空白。ANOVA 将 Figma 中的组件规范提取为结构化的 JSON 或 YAML——不是通过让 LLM 解读设计，而是确定性地读取 Figma 的组件数据，产出干净、完整的规范。

为什么确定性很重要？因为 LLM 是不一致的。让 GPT 或 Claude 描述同一个 Figma 组件两次，你会得到不同的属性名、不同的层级、不同的详细程度。Curtis 称之为「重命名问题」。ANOVA 通过在提取步骤中完全不涉及 LLM 来消除这个问题。

数据很惊人：Figma REST API 为一个典型组件暴露了 14,400+ 个属性——大多数是冗余或继承的。ANOVA 将其精简为仅有语义相关的属性，遵循四个原则：确定性、完整性、简洁性、人类可读性。

七个用例，一个底层模式

Curtis 列出了七个应用场景：为 LLM 提示注入准确的组件数据、跟踪版本变更、分析组件库覆盖度、质量检查、开发交接、自动生成文档、以及往返生成（设计→代码→设计）。底层模式始终相同：关于组件是什么以及如何运作的单一结构化真相源。

现在该怎么做

  • 用机器可读性的视角审视你的组件文档。AI 模型能仅凭你现有的文档正确使用你的组件吗？
  • 在几个核心组件上试用 ANOVA，并将其输出与你现有的交接规范对比。差异会揭示你一直在隐含传达哪些结构化信息。
  • 开始用约束而非指南来思考。「使用充裕的留白」是指南；min-gap: 16px; context: content-card 是约束。AI 智能体需要的是后者。

设计系统回答了「如何保持一致」；产品生成系统回答了「如何让 AI 用我们的组件来创造」。这个转变已经开始——现在就结构化自己规范的团队将获得显著的先发优势。

Sources:

  • https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/product-system-design
  • https://medium.com/@nathanacurtis/anova-figma-plugin
  • https://nathanacurtis.substack.com
  • https://smashingconf.com/amsterdam-2026
